stem: During pre-transplant nutritional counseling, a candidate asks why diet teaching matters after transplant. Which post-transplant disorder risk should the coordinator include in standard education?

options.text: Complete immunity to all post-transplant infections
Elimination of all cardiovascular risk after transplantation
Permanent inability to absorb any dietary fat

explanation.rationale_correct: Nutritional evaluation includes educating patients about risks for post-transplant disorders such as immunosuppressant-induced hyperlipidemia and diabetes mellitus, supporting a heart-healthy diet.

rationale_incorrect.B: Immunosuppression increases infection susceptibility rather than conferring complete immunity.
rationale_incorrect.C: Transplantation and immunosuppression do not eliminate cardiovascular risk; diet teaching addresses ongoing lipid and metabolic risks.
rationale_incorrect.D: Nutritional teaching addresses metabolic risks such as hyperlipidemia, not permanent fat malabsorption for all recipients.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: educating the patient about risks for posttransplant disorders such as immunosuppressant-induced hyperlipidemia

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 1 → H. Nutritional evaluation → 2. (post-transplant hyperlipidemia and diabetes risks; heart-healthy diet); PDF p. 32 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Fifth 010100 item; nutritional-risk angle distinct from rejection/waitlist death/primary nonfunction; anchor verified on Cupples p. 32.

stem: A potential living kidney donor asks about long-term kidney health after donation. Which counseling point aligns with standard living donor education?

options.text: Most donors have minimal end-stage renal disease risk if they maintain a healthy lifestyle
Donation guarantees development of dialysis-dependent kidney failure within one year
Living donors require lifelong immunosuppression after nephrectomy
Donors never need any post-donation medical follow-up

explanation.rationale_correct: Studies show most living kidney donors lead normal lives with a single kidney and have minimal risk of end-stage renal disease when they maintain a healthy lifestyle.

rationale_incorrect.B: Kidney donation is not associated with guaranteed early dialysis-dependent failure for most donors.
rationale_incorrect.C: Living kidney donors do not receive recipient immunosuppression after donation.
rationale_incorrect.D: Living donors commit to postoperative follow-up testing coordinated by the live donor program.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 7, Care of Living Donors → Introduction → 4.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: minimal risk of end-stage renal disease (ESRD) providing they lead a healthy lifestyle

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 7 → Introduction → 4. (living kidney donor ESRD risk with healthy lifestyle); PDF p. 331 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Fifth 010300 item; long-term ESRD-risk angle distinct from psychosocial (cctc-1023) and wound monitoring (cctc-1014); anchor verified on Cupples p. 331.

stem: A coordinator is revising long-term immunosuppression side-effect teaching. Evaluate the following statements:

elements.text: Hyperlipidemia may develop as a side effect of immunosuppressive medications.
Hypertension may develop as a side effect of certain immunosuppressants.
Immunosuppression never contributes to renal dysfunction over time.
Renal dysfunction may progress to renal failure requiring kidney transplantation.

explanation.rationale_correct: Long-term immunosuppression teaching includes hyperlipidemia and hypertension as medication side effects and notes that renal dysfunction may progress to renal failure requiring kidney transplantation. Immunosuppression can contribute to renal dysfunction.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement IV is also correct—renal dysfunction may progress to need for kidney transplantation.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement III is false; medications and other factors may contribute to renal dysfunction over time.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement III is false; not all four statements are correct.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 3, Patient Education → j. Long-term effects of immunosuppression
primary_anchor.quote_hint: Hyperlipidemia … Hypertension … Renal dysfunction … May progress to renal failure

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 3 → j. Long-term effects of immunosuppression → ii.–iv. (hypertension, hyperlipidemia, renal dysfunction); PDF p. 120 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Synthesized item. Seventh complex_combo in bank; anchor verified on Cupples p. 120.

stem: Per OPTN and CMS requirements, who may perform the living donor psychosocial evaluation?

options.text: A psychiatrist, psychologist, masters-prepared social worker, or licensed clinical social worker
Only the transplant surgeon without any behavioral health specialist
Any hospital volunteer without clinical licensure
The recipient's primary care physician exclusively

explanation.rationale_correct: The living donor psychosocial evaluation must be performed by a psychiatrist, psychologist, masters-prepared social worker, or licensed clinical social worker per OPTN and CMS requirements.

rationale_incorrect.B: Psychosocial evaluation requires qualified behavioral health professionals, not the surgeon alone.
rationale_incorrect.C: Volunteers without clinical licensure cannot perform the required psychosocial evaluation.
rationale_incorrect.D: The recipient's primary care physician is not the designated evaluator for living donor psychosocial assessment.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 7, Care of Living Donors → A. The Psychosocial Evaluation → 1.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: psychosocial evaluation must be performed by a psychiatrist, psychologist, masters-prepared social worker, or licensed clinical social worker
